p.src: What a Measurement Can Return

u.src: What a Measurement Can Return
en: What a Measurement Can Return

p.src: An observable is something that can be measured. The established word is slightly grander than necessary; measurable would have served just as well. To every observable we associate a Hermitian operator. Let $L$ denote such an operator for now: $L^\dagger=L.$ Not every linear operator is Hermitian. Conversely, whether a particular Hermitian operator can be measured with available materials and apparatus may be a difficult experimental question. The abstract working rule is nevertheless generous: a Hermitian operator represents a possible observable, even if the practical measurement has not yet been invented.

p.src: If $L\ket{\lambda}=\lambda\ket{\lambda},$ then $\lambda$ is a possible numerical result of measuring $L$. We use the same symbol to label the eigenvalue and its eigenvector. The ket bars distinguish the two: $\lambda$ is a number, while $\ket{\lambda}$ is a state.

p.src: Why Hermitian operators? A primitive apparatus reports real numbers. If an instrument appears to report one complex number, it is really reporting two independent real quantities. Thus observable eigenvalues must be real. Moreover, states associated with different definite outcomes must be physically distinguishable and hence orthogonal. In the finite-dimensional setting used here, a linear operator with a complete orthonormal eigenbasis and real eigenvalues is Hermitian. The physical statements and the Hermitian structure therefore fit one another.

p.src: Distinguishability Is Orthogonality

u.src: Distinguishability Is Orthogonality
en: Distinguishability Is Orthogonality

p.src: The phrase physically distinguishable has an operational meaning. Suppose a spin is prepared either up or down. A measurement along the $z$-axis separates the possibilities without ambiguity: up gives $+1$, down gives $-1$. Likewise, left and right can be distinguished by measuring along the $x$-axis.

en: The phrase physically distinguishable has an operational meaning. Suppose a spin is prepared either up or down. p.src: Now suppose the preparation is either up or right. A $z$-measurement gives $+1$ with certainty for up, but the right state also gives $+1$ with nonzero probability. An $x$-measurement merely reverses the asymmetry. Tilting the apparatus by $45^\circ$ does not remove the overlap between the outcome distributions. No orientation produces a result that always distinguishes the two preparations.

p.src: Born’s Rule

u.src: Born’s Rule
en: Born’s Rule

p.src: The eigenvalues tell us what may happen, but not how often. The probability rule supplies the predictive content. If a normalized system is prepared in $\ket{A}$, and a normalized eigenvector $\ket{\lambda}$ belongs to the measured observable $L$, then $P(\lambda)=\left|\braket{\lambda}{A}\right|^2.$ The overlap $\braket{\lambda}{A}$ is a probability amplitude. It is generally complex, so it cannot itself be a probability. Its absolute square is real and nonnegative.

p.src: Born’s rule written beside the measurement principles: probability is the absolute square of an overlap.

u.src: Born’s rule written beside the measurement principles: probability is the absolute square of an overlap.
en: Born’s rule written beside the measurement principles: probability is the absolute square of an overlap.

caption.en: Born’s rule written beside the measurement principles: probability is the absolute square of an overlap.

p.src:
Choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $L$ and expand $\ket{A}=\sum_i \alpha_i\ket{\lambda_i},
\qquad
\alpha_i=\braket{\lambda_i}{A}.$ Born’s rule becomes $P(\lambda_i)=|\alpha_i|^2.$ Normalization then gives $\sum_i P(\lambda_i)=\sum_i|\alpha_i|^2=1.$ The positivity and normalization requirements do not by themselves derive Born’s rule, but they show why the absolute square fits probability theory so naturally. Ultimately the rule is tested by experiment.

p.src: Degenerate Outcomes

u.src: Degenerate Outcomes
en: Degenerate Outcomes

p.src:
An eigenvalue may belong to more than one independent eigenvector. Suppose $\begin{aligned}
L\ket{\lambda,1}&=\lambda\ket{\lambda,1},\\
L\ket{\lambda,2}&=\lambda\ket{\lambda,2}.\end{aligned}$ Every linear combination in their span is also an eigenvector with eigenvalue $\lambda$: $L\bigl(\alpha\ket{\lambda,1}+\beta\ket{\lambda,2}\bigr)
=
\lambda\bigl(\alpha\ket{\lambda,1}+\beta\ket{\lambda,2}\bigr).$ This freedom lets us choose an orthonormal basis inside the degenerate eigenspace. If the label $a$ runs over that basis, the probability of the numerical outcome $\lambda$ is the sum over its mutually exclusive orthogonal channels: $P(\lambda)=\sum_a\left|\braket{\lambda,a}{A}\right|^2.$ Equivalently, if $P_\lambda$ is the projector onto the full eigenspace, then $P(\lambda)=\bra{A}P_\lambda\ket{A}$. The projector notation is compact; Equation  displays the probability addition directly.

p.src: The New Question: How States Change

u.src: The New Question: How States Change
en: The New Question: How States Change

p.src: The preceding principles specify states and measurements. Dynamics asks what happens between one time and another. The classical analogy is useful. A two-state coin might remain unchanged at every tick, or it might alternate heads, tails, heads, tails. A six-sided die admits more update rules, and a continuous state space admits infinitely many. A dynamical law maps the present state to the next one.

p.src: A satisfactory classical law is deterministic and reversible. Distinct states do not merge into one state, because if they did the present would no longer determine the past. This preservation of information is sometimes called the minus first law: it comes before the more familiar conservation laws.

p.src: The quantum version begins with a state vector $\ket{\psi(t)}$, explicitly regarded as a function of time. Postulate a single linear time-development operator $U(t)$ such that $\ket{\psi(t)}=U(t)\ket{\psi(0)}.$ The same $U(t)$ acts on every initial state of the system. It is not chosen afresh according to the input vector, and its action is linear. More general nonlinear or state-dependent laws can be imagined, but they rapidly conflict with the probabilistic, causal, and composite-system structure of quantum mechanics.

p.src: Reversibility Preserves Overlaps

u.src: Reversibility Preserves Overlaps
en: Reversibility Preserves Overlaps

p.src:
Let a second initial state evolve by the same law: $\ket{\phi(t)}=U(t)\ket{\phi(0)}.$ If the two preparations are distinguishable initially, they must remain distinguishable. Therefore $\braket{\psi(0)}{\phi(0)}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\braket{\psi(t)}{\phi(t)}=0.$

p.src: Two states evolve under the same $U(t)$; initial orthogonality remains orthogonality.

u.src: Two states evolve under the same $U(t)$; initial orthogonality remains orthogonality.

p.src: Preserving normalized states and orthogonality is strong enough to preserve all inner products. To see the mechanism, expand two arbitrary vectors in an orthonormal basis. The basis vectors remain orthonormal under the evolution, so the coefficients reconstruct the same overlap at every time: $\braket{\psi(t)}{\phi(t)}=\braket{\psi(0)}{\phi(0)}.$ Thus not only complete distinguishability but the entire degree of similarity between two states is conserved.

p.src: Infinitesimal Time and the Hamiltonian

u.src: Infinitesimal Time and the Hamiltonian
en: Infinitesimal Time and the Hamiltonian

p.src:
At zero elapsed time nothing changes, so $U(0)=I$. For a very small interval $\epsilon$, $U(\epsilon)$ must be close to the identity. In units that temporarily set $\hbar=1$, write $U(\epsilon)=I-i\epsilon H+O(\epsilon^2).$ The minus sign and factor of $i$ are initially conventions; without knowing $H$, they can be absorbed into its definition. Their usefulness appears when unitarity is imposed. Hermitian conjugation gives $U^\dagger(\epsilon)=I+i\epsilon H^\dagger+O(\epsilon^2).$ Then $\begin{aligned}
I
&=U^\dagger(\epsilon)U(\epsilon)\\
&=\bigl(I+i\epsilon H^\dagger\bigr)
  \bigl(I-i\epsilon H\bigr)+O(\epsilon^2)\\
&=I+i\epsilon(H^\dagger-H)+O(\epsilon^2).\end{aligned}$ The first-order term must vanish: $H^\dagger=H.$

p.src: The letter $H$ stands not for Hermitian but for Hamiltonian. Since it is Hermitian, it represents an observable. It is identified with the energy and, more structurally, with the generator of time translations. The identification is not exhausted by a name: in systems with a known classical limit, the quantum $H$ must reproduce the classical Hamiltonian’s dynamics. Symmetry, the degrees of freedom, physical judgment, and ultimately experiment determine which Hermitian operator is the Hamiltonian of a particular system.

p.src: The Hamiltonian may depend explicitly on time. A magnetic field whose current is being varied supplies a simple example. If the external parameters are time independent, then $H$ has no explicit time dependence; this is time-translation invariance. If the parameters are driven in time, the energy need not be conserved.

p.src:
Apply Equation  to the state: $\ket{\psi(\epsilon)}=(I-i\epsilon H)\ket{\psi(0)}+O(\epsilon^2).$ Rearranging and dividing by $\epsilon$, $\frac{\ket{\psi(\epsilon)}-\ket{\psi(0)}}{\epsilon}
=-iH\ket{\psi(0)}+O(\epsilon).$

p.src: The infinitesimal state update rearranged into a vector-valued difference quotient.

u.src: The infinitesimal state update rearranged into a vector-valued difference quotient.

caption.en: The infinitesimal state update rearranged into a vector-valued difference quotient.

p.src:
There is no special mystery in differentiating a vector. Two vectors can be subtracted, their difference can be divided by a number, and the limit defines another vector. The reference time called zero above can be any instant. Taking $\epsilon\to0$ therefore yields $\boxed{\frac{d}{dt}\ket{\psi(t)}=-iH\ket{\psi(t)}}
\qquad(\hbar=1).$

p.src: This is the generalized time-dependent Schrödinger equation. The familiar differential equation for a particle’s wavefunction is one representation of this abstract state-vector equation. To use it, one must know $H$ and the initial state.

p.src:
For a finite interval, solve the differential equation. When $H$ is time independent, repeatedly composing infinitesimal steps gives $U(t)=e^{-iHt}
\qquad(\hbar=1),$ which is the precise version of composing all the small steps. Time-dependent Hamiltonians require time ordering, a refinement we postpone.

p.src: Restoring Planck’s Constant

u.src: Restoring Planck’s Constant
en: Restoring Planck’s Constant

p.src: The preceding equation used units where $\hbar=1$. Dimensional analysis shows where $\hbar$ belongs. The derivative has dimensions of inverse time, while $H$ has dimensions of energy. Since $\hbar$ has dimensions energy times time, $\boxed{i\hbar\frac{d}{dt}\ket{\psi(t)}=H\ket{\psi(t)}}.$ Equivalently, the infinitesimal operator is $U(\epsilon)=I-i\epsilon H/\hbar+O(\epsilon^2)$, and the finite time-independent evolution is $U(t)=e^{-iHt/\hbar}$.

en: Expectation Value Means Average

p.src: To compare quantum dynamics with classical equations, we need the average value of an observable. The standard name expectation value is potentially misleading. For a fair variable taking only $+1$ and $-1$, the average is zero although zero is never observed. A symmetric distribution can even vanish throughout a neighborhood of its mean. The mean, median, and mode coincide for some smooth, single-peaked distributions, but not in general.

p.src: Repeated trials connect the mathematical mean to data. Under the usual independence and finite-moment assumptions, laws of large numbers state probabilistic convergence of the sample average. They do not guarantee that every finite sequence lies close to the mean; an extraordinarily long run of identical spin outcomes remains possible, merely improbable. This is the same statistical subtlety that prevents the second law of thermodynamics from being an exceptionless microscopic prohibition.

p.src: The Operator Sandwich

u.src: The Operator Sandwich
en: The Operator Sandwich

p.src:
Expand a normalized state in an orthonormal eigenbasis of $L$: $\ket{A}=\sum_i\alpha_i\ket{\lambda_i},
\qquad
\bra{A}=\sum_j\alpha_j^*\bra{\lambda_j}.$ Born’s rule and Equation  give $\overline{\lambda}=\sum_i\lambda_i|\alpha_i|^2.$ Now calculate $\begin{aligned}
\bra{A}L\ket{A}
&=\sum_{i,j}\alpha_j^*\alpha_i
  \bra{\lambda_j}L\ket{\lambda_i}\\
&=\sum_{i,j}\alpha_j^*\alpha_i\lambda_i
  \braket{\lambda_j}{\lambda_i}\\
&=\sum_i\lambda_i|\alpha_i|^2.\end{aligned}$ The double sum collapses because $\braket{\lambda_j}{\lambda_i}=\delta_{ji}$. Hence $\boxed{\expect{L}_A=\bra{A}L\ket{A}}.$

p.src: Angle brackets and an overbar will both be used for averages. When the state evolves, $\expect{L}_t=\bra{\psi(t)}L\ket{\psi(t)}.$ The subscript only reminds us that the state, and therefore the average, depends on time. In the present Schrödinger-picture discussion, $L$ itself is fixed unless explicit time dependence is stated.

p.src:
Operators need not commute. Their order matters just as matrix order matters. Define $=HL-LH.$ Then $\boxed{\frac{d}{dt}\expect{L}=i\expect{[H,L]}}
\qquad(\hbar=1).$

p.src: Dirac recognized this connection and used it as a route into quantum mechanics. It must nevertheless be handled as a correspondence, not a universal substitution rule: operator-ordering ambiguities can appear, and the classical limit must be derived from quantum dynamics. Conceptually, quantum mechanics comes first; classical mechanics is its approximation for suitable states and scales. Commutators precede Poisson brackets, even though the historical analogy helps us discover the relation.

p.src: Average Energy Is Conserved

u.src: Average Energy Is Conserved
en: Average Energy Is Conserved

p.src:
Take $L=H$ in Equation , with a time-independent Hamiltonian: $\frac{d}{dt}\expect{H}
=\frac{i}{\hbar}\expect{[H,H]}.$ Every operator commutes with itself, $=HH-HH=0,$ so $\boxed{\frac{d}{dt}\expect{H}=0}.$

p.src: This proves a deliberately modest statement: the average energy is constant. A stronger statement about the entire energy distribution will follow from the same dynamics. If $H$ depends explicitly on time, the extra explicit derivative need not vanish and the driven system can exchange energy with whatever changes its parameters.
